The Common linnet (Linaria cannabina) is a small passerine that exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in adult body mass. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 18.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 18.7 grams], while males are notably heavier, reaching a maximum adult mass of 20.5 grams [Wwi = 20.5 grams]. This difference likely reflects sexual selection pressures on male body size during territory and mate acquisition. At hatching, altricial nestlings emerge from the calcareous egg at a remarkably small size; neonatal body mass has been recorded at just 1.11 grams [Wwb = 1.11 grams], a value consistent with the extreme altriciality characteristic of cardueline finches. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, prior to any embryonic development, is approximately 1.9 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.9 grams], indicating that the egg represents a substantial maternal investment relative to the hatchling's subsequent mass. Incubation duration is tightly linked to thermal conditions; eggs maintained at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] require an incubation period of 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days] before pipping occurs, a developmental schedule typical of temperate-zone carduelids.

During this nestling stage, the downy chick undergoes rapid mass gain, progressing from its modest birth weight toward the adult asymptotic mass. The transition to nutritional independence follows the achievement of first flight, after which the fledgling begins to forage on seeds and small invertebrates. Comparative studies indicate that the fledging period of the linnet is somewhat compressed relative to that of larger-bodied fringillid finches, likely reflecting the selective pressures of a short breeding season in temperate habitats.

This early maturation is typical of many small-bodied cardueline finches, which often face intense competition for limited breeding territories. The age at which individuals initiate their first reproductive effort, however, is delayed substantially beyond the point of mere physiological readiness. Field data indicate that first brood production occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a full year after the chick leaves the nest at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between puberty and first reproduction likely reflects the time required for young birds to acquire a territory, establish a pair bond, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation.

Females capable of sustained breeding effort may complete up to 2.5 nesting attempts per year [F_R_i = up to 2.5 nesting attempts per year], though this maximum reproductive rate is only achieved under favorable environmental conditions with adequate food supply and low predation pressure. The total annual output from a breeding pair can exceed 12 eggs per year under optimal circumstances, though fledging success is highly variable depending on local predator abundance and weather patterns.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the species, measured under the active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 9.4 years [am = approximately 9.4 years], a value that falls within the range observed for other small-bodied cardueline finches. This relatively extended lifespan for a bird weighing no more than 20.5 grams may reflect a bet-hedging strategy in which individuals spread reproductive effort across multiple breeding seasons, mitigating the impact of occasional catastrophic reproductive failure.
